h1: The 7 Best Server Racks Under $300 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Server Racks Under $300: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: seven budget server racks and wall-mount cabinets under $300, compared on rack units, depth, load rating, doors and mounting.
summary: The VEVOR 12U Open Frame is our top pick because it combines adjustable depth and a strong load rating at one of the lowest buckets here. The NavePoint 12U glass-door cabinet is the tidy enclosed option, the Tecmojo 6U wall cabinet is the lockable space saver, and the RIVECO 4U wall rack is the pick for a switch-only closet.
intro: Cheap racks tempt you to buy the biggest number, but the cost of a wrong rack at this price is mostly wasted space. A closet with a router, a switch and a NAS needs four to six units, not twelve, and a twelve-unit frame will stand half empty in a spot you could have used for storage. Matching the rack to the gear you own today, plus modest headroom, is what separates a clean install from a regret.

We ranked seven racks that all sit well below $300 on frame, size and mounting. Wall-mount racks keep floors clear, open frames cool best, and enclosed cabinets hide and protect equipment. The listings are short on load figures, with exceptions such as the 80 kg rating on the RIVECO, so we note where a rating is missing and rank on the details that are stated.

products.name: VEVOR 12U Open Frame Server Rack
products.verdict: A 12U open frame with adjustable depth and strong load capacity in the $50 to $100 bucket.
products.description:
The VEVOR 12U skips doors and panels entirely: twelve units of bare rails, rear posts that slide to change depth, and a listing that promises a high weight rating. Adjustable depth is the standout, because it lets the rear posts move to match a shallow switch or a deeper server.

It takes first place because 12U with adjustable depth at $50 to $100 beats every enclosed cabinet on flexibility per dollar. The NavePoint 12U offers a glass door and a tidier look, but costs more and fixes its depth.

A strong choice for a garage, closet or office corner. The caveat is the open design: there is no door, no lock and no dust protection, so it suits rooms you control.
products.idealFor: Garages, closets and offices where cooling matters.
products.skipIf: You need a locked or enclosed rack.

products.name: NavePoint 12U Server Rack Enclosure with Glass Door
products.verdict: A 12U IT cabinet with a glass front and removable side panels.
products.description:
NavePoint's 12U cabinet has a glass front door and removable side panels, with a durable build. The glass lets you see status lights, and the side panels come off when you need to run cables.

It ranks second because an enclosed cabinet is neater and quieter than the VEVOR frame, but it costs more and traps heat. It beats the smaller NavePoint 9U on capacity, which matters when you add a second device.

Good for a living-room or office installation where the rack stays visible. The caveat is airflow, so a closed cabinet needs a fan if the gear runs warm.
products.idealFor: Visible installs in living or office spaces.
products.skipIf: You run hot servers without fans.

products.name: Tecmojo 6U Wall Mount Server Cabinet IT Network Rack Enclosure Lockable Door
products.verdict: A 6U wall-mount cabinet with a lockable door that keeps network gear off the floor.
products.description:
Tecmojo's 6U cabinet mounts on the wall to save floor space, locks to keep network equipment secure and is built for easy equipment configuration. Six units fit a modem, router, switch and patch panel with room to spare.

It ranks third because it combines security and a small footprint, which the open frames cannot, though 6U limits expansion. It sits above the RIVECO 4U because it adds a door.

Best for an apartment, a hallway closet or a small office. The caveat is that the cabinet loads weight onto the wall, so mount it to studs or masonry.
products.idealFor: Apartments and small offices with limited floor space.
products.skipIf: You plan to add servers or a UPS.

products.name: RIVECO 4U 19" Wall Mount Network Rack, 17.7" Deep 2 Post Open Frame Cabinet
products.verdict: A 4U two-post wall rack in SPCC steel with an 80 kg load rating.
products.description:
RIVECO's 4U rack is a two-post open frame for the wall, 17.7 inches deep and 11 inches tall, built from heavy-duty SPCC cold-rolled steel with an 80 kg load capacity. An 80 kg figure is unusually specific among budget racks.

It ranks fourth because 4U holds only a switch, a patch panel and a small device, whereas the Tecmojo adds a door and extra space. It beats the larger open frames on how little room it consumes.

A fit for a home network closet or a hall cupboard. The caveat is depth: 17.7 inches rejects deep servers, so it is for networking gear only.
products.idealFor: Home network closets with a switch and patch panel.
products.skipIf: You own servers or need a door.

products.name: AxcessAbles 12U Network Rack with Wheels
products.verdict: A steel 12U rack on wheels with universal 19 inch compatibility.
products.description:
AxcessAbles offers a 12U steel rack on wheels that accepts universal 19 inch gear and claims heavy-duty load capacity. Wheels let you pull the rack out to reach the rear, which is a real help for cabling.

It ranks fifth because the VEVOR gives similar height for less, with adjustable depth, and the AxcessAbles listing gives no depth or load figure. It wins on mobility, which neither open frame offers.

Good for a workshop or studio where the rack moves. The caveat is that wheels need locking casters in use, and loaded racks can be top-heavy.
products.idealFor: Workshops and studios where the rack must move.
products.skipIf: You want adjustable depth or a lock.

products.name: NavePoint 9U Server Rack Enclosure with Glass Door
products.verdict: A 9U enclosed cabinet with a glass door and removable side panels.
products.description:
The NavePoint 9U is a smaller version of the 12U, with the same glass door and removable side panels and a durable, convenient design. Nine units suit a switch, a patch panel, a small server and a UPS.

It ranks sixth because the 12U cabinet gives three more units for the same bucket of $100 to $200, so the 9U is only worth it if space is tight. It remains a fair choice for a desk-side install.

The pick for a compact enclosed rack. The caveat is that capacity runs out fast, and glass doors still need ventilation.

products.name: ZHPHMBM 12U Server Rack Cabinet
products.verdict: A 12U cabinet pitched on sturdy construction, space saving and a ventilation design.
products.description:
ZHPHMBM sells a 12U cabinet with a sturdy build, a space-saving layout and a ventilation design. The ventilation mention is the useful one, since enclosed racks overheat without airflow paths.

It ranks seventh because the listing is the vaguest in the group, with no door type, depth or load figure, and the brand has little history. It stays on the list as a 12U enclosed option in the $100 to $200 bucket.

Suits a buyer who wants a vented cabinet and will verify the details. The caveat is that vague listings invite surprises, so read the dimensions before you order.
products.idealFor: Enclosed 12U installs where airflow is a priority.
products.skipIf: You need documented depth and load ratings.

whatMatters.detail: A rack unit is 1.75 inches of height. A modem, router, switch and patch panel typically fill four to six units, and a small server adds two. Count what you own, then add a few spare units. Check the listed U rating against that count so a cheap rack does not run out of space immediately.

Wall racks free the floor but hang their weight on studs or masonry, while floor racks carry weight on their own legs. A loaded wall cabinet is heavy. Check the stated load rating, locate studs before ordering and avoid drywall-only mounting for anything with a UPS.

Servers and NAS boxes vary from shallow to very deep. Adjustable posts let the rack accept either. A fixed 17.7 inch depth suits switches only. Look for the word adjustable depth or a stated depth range, and compare it with the deepest device you plan to mount.

Doors keep dust and curious hands out, and a lock protects equipment in shared spaces. They also trap heat. Check whether the listing names a lock and a vented panel, and decide based on where the rack sits and how much power your gear draws.

The rack must carry every device, plus a UPS if you have one. Listings often skip this number. An 80 kg rating, as on the RIVECO, is specific and testable. Check for a figure in kilograms or pounds, and place the heaviest items at the bottom.

faq.q: How many rack units do I need for a home network?
faq.a: Four to six for a modem, router, switch and patch panel. The RIVECO 4U or Tecmojo 6U cover that. Add a NAS or UPS and you want 9U to 12U, like the NavePoint or VEVOR.

faq.q: What mistake do people make with budget racks?
faq.a: Ignoring depth. A shallow wall rack like the RIVECO, at 17.7 inches, suits switches but not servers. Buy the VEVOR with adjustable depth if you may add deeper gear later.

faq.q: Is the NavePoint 12U worth more than the VEVOR?
faq.a: Only if appearance and dust protection matter. The NavePoint adds a glass door and side panels, while the VEVOR gives adjustable depth and better airflow for a lower bucket.

faq.q: How do I mount a wall cabinet safely?
faq.a: Find wall studs or use masonry anchors, mount the empty cabinet first, then load gear from the bottom. The Tecmojo 6U and RIVECO 4U both hang their weight on the wall, so drywall alone will not do.
They can. A glass-door cabinet like the NavePoint traps heat from servers, so add a fan or choose the vented ZHPHMBM. Network switches run cool, but servers and UPS units need airflow.

faq.q: Can I roll a loaded rack?
faq.a: Carefully. The AxcessAbles has wheels, but a loaded rack is top-heavy, so keep heavy gear low, lock the casters when parked and roll slowly over thresholds.

finalTake: The VEVOR 12U Open Frame is the best server rack under $300 because it pairs adjustable depth with 12U at a low bucket. Pick the NavePoint 12U for a tidy glass-door look, the Tecmojo 6U for a locked wall cabinet and the RIVECO 4U if all you own is a switch. Match units to your gear first.
